questions.lesson_line: Always weigh how often you win by how much you win or lose.

wrong.B, at +0.35R a trade: That counts B's wins and forgets its losses.
wrong.B, because it wins more: Winning often isn't enough when each loss is four times a win.
wrong.A, at +1.2R a trade: That's A's winners alone. Take off the losers.

questions.simple: Plan A is better at +0.5R a trade, because its big wins pay for its losses while B's big losses sink it.

deeper.trap: Plan B feels better to trade, because it wins 70% of the time. But it loses the other 30%, and each 2R loss costs four 0.5R wins. Tharp notes some systems that win often still lose money through occasional large losses. Always weigh how often by how much.

questions.q: Which term means the share of your closed trades that made money?
questions.why: Win rate. Tharp defines it as the percentage of closed trades in which you make money. Investopedia agrees: winning trades out of all trades. It says how often you win, never how much.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate counts how often you win. It never says how much.

wrong.Expectancy: That's your average result per trade, which weighs the size of wins and losses too.
wrong.R-multiple: That's one trade's result counted in R.
wrong.Risk/reward ratio: That's about one trade's plan, not your record of closed trades.

questions.simple: Win rate, because it counts how often your closed trades made money, not how much.

questions.story: Over 100 trades, 99 lose $1 each. One trade makes $500.
questions.q: Your win rate is 1%. What is the net result?
questions.why: A $401 profit. The 99 losers cost $1 each, $99 in all. The one winner made $500, and $500 less $99 is $401. This is Tharp's own example: 99% of the trades lost and the method still made money. Win rate counts how often you win, never how much.
questions.lesson_line: A low win rate can pay and a high one can lose. Check the sizes.

wrong.A $99 loss: That counts the losers and forgets the one big winner.
wrong.A $4.01 gain: That's the average per trade, the $401 spread over 100 trades. The question asks for the net result.

questions.simple: You net a $401 profit, because the one $500 winner is bigger than the 99 losses of $1.

deeper.counter: It works the other way too. Investopedia: if the losses are three times as large as the gains, more wins than losses is still a losing strategy. Win rate alone proves nothing.

reasons: one publisher only (Van Tharp Institute) for the key

questions.q: What does a trade's risk/reward ratio compare?
choices: Loss at the stop vs gain at the target
Your winning trades vs your losers
Your risk vs your account size
Today's range vs the average range
questions.answer: Loss at the stop vs gain at the target
questions.why: Loss at the stop vs gain at the target. Investopedia measures entry to the stop against entry to the take-profit order. Tharp says to ask before every trade whether the reward is worth the risk. It describes one trade's plan, not your record of wins and losses.
questions.lesson_line: Before you buy, know both distances: to the stop and to the target.

wrong.Your winning trades vs your losers: That's a count of wins and losses, not one trade's setup.
wrong.Your risk vs your account size: That's your risk per trade as a share of the account. Risk/reward compares two distances on one trade.
wrong.Today's range vs the average range: That's a volatility read. ATR is the stock's average range of movement per day.

questions.simple: It compares what you lose if the stop is hit with what you gain if the target is reached.

questions.q: Entry $20, stop $19, target $23. How many dollars can you make for each dollar you risk?
questions.why: $3. The target is $23 less $20 away. The stop is $20 less $19 away. The target is three times as far. Investopedia writes that as 1:3 risk/reward: three units of reward for every unit of risk.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the distance to the target by the distance to the stop.
questions.simple: You can make $3 for each $1 you risk, because the target is three times as far away as the stop.

questions.story: You buy at $20 with a target of $30. To improve the ratio, you move your stop from $15 up to $18.
questions.q: What did the tighter stop cost you?
choices: More chance the stop is hit
questions.answer: More chance the stop is hit
questions.why: More chance the stop is hit. Moving the stop from $15 to $18 cuts the loss per share and improves the ratio to the $30 target. But a stop closer to entry is more likely to be triggered by normal price swings. So the better ratio comes with a lower chance of reaching the target.
questions.lesson_line: A tighter stop makes the ratio look better and the stop easier to hit.

wrong.Nothing, the trade got safer: The loss per share shrank, but the odds of being stopped out went up.
wrong.Some of your upside to $30: The target didn't move. Only the stop did.
wrong.Your protection from a gap: No stop protects against a gap, at $15 or at $18.

questions.simple: It raised the chance the stop is hit, because a stop closer to your entry is easier for normal swings to reach.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a trade by its ratio alone. Pulling the stop up makes the ratio look better on paper. It does that by moving the stop closer to normal swings. Our rule is stop first, and the size comes from the stop.

questions.q: What does position sizing decide?
questions.why: How many shares to buy. Investopedia: position sizing decides how many units to invest, given your account size and risk tolerance. Tharp calls it the part of your system that says how much you trade. Size comes from the stop distance. So sizing does not pick the stock, the stop or the exit.
questions.lesson_line: The stop comes first. Position sizing turns it into a share count.

wrong.Where to put your stop: The stop comes first, from the chart. Sizing uses its distance.
wrong.Which stock to buy: That's your setup and your watchlist.

questions.simple: How many shares to buy, because sizing turns your stop and your risk into a share count.

questions.q: Account $40,000, risking 1% a trade. Entry $25, stop $23.50. How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 266 shares. Take 1% of $40,000. Divide it by the risk per share, $25 less $23.50. Round down, never up. Investopedia's method is the same: account risk divided by trade risk gives the share count. Our rule then caps it: the size is the smaller of this and the position cap, 40% of the account. Here the cap does not bind.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk divided by risk per share. Round down, never up.
questions.simple: Buy 266 shares, because 1% of the account divided by your risk per share, rounded down, gives 266.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)

questions.q: What does the 2% rule limit?
choices: Your risk per trade to 2% of capital
Each position to 2% of the account
Your stop to 2% under your entry price
Your losses in any one month to 2%
questions.answer: Your risk per trade to 2% of capital
questions.why: Your risk per trade to 2% of capital. The rule caps what you plan to lose if the stop is hit, not how much you buy. A 2% risk can sit on a much bigger position. Gaps and slippage can still push a real loss past 2%. UCT's absolute ceiling is also 2%.
questions.lesson_line: The 2% rule caps risk, not position size.

wrong.Each position to 2% of the account: That mixes up risk and size. A 2% risk can sit on a much bigger position.
wrong.Your stop to 2% under your entry price: The rule caps the dollars you lose. The chart sets where the stop goes.
wrong.Your losses in any one month to 2%: A monthly cap is a separate rule. UCT's monthly loss limit is 8%.

questions.simple: It caps your risk on one trade at 2% of capital, what you plan to lose at the stop.

deeper.counter: A 2% risk does not mean a 2% position. In Tharp's magazine example you buy $10,000 of stock, yet your initial risk is only $1,000. The stop distance sets how big the position can be.

reasons: the why names the owner's rulebook A1 ceiling (2%)
fixed before (key changed from loss to risk)

questions.q: What is gap risk for a position with a stop?
choices: Your stop sits too far away
questions.why: Price opens past your stop. A gap through the stop still triggers it, and the stock sells at the next available price. So the loss can be well beyond what you planned. Investopedia notes that even proper position sizing cannot prevent it. Schwab: after a gap down, the fill can be far below the stop price.
questions.lesson_line: A stop picks when you sell, not the price you get in a gap.

wrong.Your stop sits too far away: That's a stop-placement choice. Gap risk is price jumping past the stop.
wrong.The stock drifts sideways: That costs you time, not a gap.
wrong.Your order fills in parts: That's a partial fill, an order issue.

questions.simple: Price jumps past your stop at the open, so the stop sells lower than planned and you lose more.

questions.story: You risk 1% of the account. Entry $170, with a stop order at $155 resting with your broker. Bad news hits overnight, and the stock opens at $140.
questions.q: Roughly how much of the account did you lose?
choices: None yet, the gap skipped it
About 18%, as far as it fell
questions.why: About 2%, twice your plan. Your resting stop became a market order at the open and sold near $140. The drop from $170 to $140 is twice your stop distance. So the loss is about twice your planned 1%. The SEC: a triggered stop's fill can be far from the stop price.
questions.lesson_line: Plan your size for the gap, not just for the stop.

wrong.None yet, the gap skipped it: A gap through the stop still triggers it. It sells at the next available price.
wrong.About 18%, as far as it fell: That's how far the stock fell, $170 to $140. Your account lost what your size made it lose, about twice the 1% you planned.
wrong.1%, your stop capped the loss: A stop can't fill at a price the stock never traded. It sold near the $140 open.

questions.simple: You lost about 2%: the stop sold at the open, and the drop to $140 was twice your stop distance.

deeper.trap: A stop is a trigger, not a floor. When a stock gaps past it, the order sells at the next available price. Investopedia warns slippage and gap risk can make a loss significantly greater than planned.

reasons: touches the owner's gap rule (B20), flagged

questions.story: You hold a stock into its earnings report tomorrow. The trade is up 2R. Your stop is $2 under the price, and a $4 gap down is possible.
questions.q: Under UCT's rule, what do you do before the report?
choices: Sell it all before the report
Halve the size and hold the rest
Hold, the stop caps the loss
questions.answer: Sell it all before the report
questions.why: Sell it all before the report. Our rule: hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. Up 2R, you are out before it. No stop protects you in a gap. A gap through the stop fills at the next available price. A $4 gap is twice your $2 stop. Halving the size, Investopedia's idea, still leaves half the position exposed.
questions.lesson_line: A stop can't stop a gap. We hold through earnings only when up 5R.

wrong.Switch to a stop-limit order: In a gap it may not fill at all, and you'd still hold the stock into the report.
wrong.Halve the size and hold the rest: That's Investopedia's way to cut gap risk. Our rule is stricter: under 5R, nothing is held through a report.
wrong.Hold, the stop caps the loss: A gap fills at the next available price, past the stop. We hold only trades up 5R.

questions.simple: Sell before the report, because our rule holds through earnings only when a trade is up 5R, and this one is up 2R.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the stop. A stop sets when you sell, not the price you get. If the stock opens $4 lower, the stop triggers and fills near the open, about twice the loss you planned. That is why our rule clears trades under 5R out before the report instead of hoping the stop holds.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B22 (hold through a report only if up 5R)
a rule the owner has already changed once (the day count)

questions.q: What job does the stop-loss do in your plan?
choices: Sets where you get out if wrong
Locks in the exact price you sell at
Picks where you will take your profit
Sets how many shares you should buy
questions.answer: Sets where you get out if wrong
questions.why: Sets where you get out if wrong. Tharp calls a stop a preplanned exit. The SEC says investors use sell stops to try to limit a loss on stock they own. It does not lock in a price. The stop price is a trigger, and the order then sells at market. It does not pick your target or your share count, though sizing uses its distance.
questions.lesson_line: Decide where you're wrong before you buy. That's the stop.

wrong.Locks in the exact price you sell at: It sets an exit, not a price. Once hit, it sells at market, and the fill can differ.
wrong.Picks where you will take your profit: That's the target, the reward side of the plan.
wrong.Sets how many shares you should buy: Sizing comes after the stop and uses its distance.

questions.simple: It sets where you get out if the trade goes wrong, so you know your exit before you buy.

questions.q: It's fine to pick your stop after the trade is already open.
questions.why: False. Tharp's golden rule: never open a position without knowing exactly where you will exit. His article says the exit that sets your worst-case risk comes before you enter. Schwab also says to specify how you'll close a trade before you place it. At UCT, every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
questions.lesson_line: No stop, no trade. The exit is part of the entry.
questions.simple: False, you set your exit before you open the trade, never after it is already on.

reasons: the why teaches the owner's rulebook D39 (entry, stop and size written down before the open)

questions.q: Our default stop on a new long is a flat 8% under your entry.
questions.why: False. Our default stop sits a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low. It comes from the chart, not from a fixed percent. The size then comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Our default stop: a few cents under today's low or yesterday's low.
questions.simple: False, because our default stop goes a few cents under today's low or yesterday's low, not a flat percent.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: What is a drawdown?
choices: A drop from a peak to a low
A loss below what you paid
Money taken out of an account
questions.answer: A drop from a peak to a low
questions.why: A drop from a peak to a low. Investopedia quotes it as the percent fall from a peak to the trough after it. Fidelity: from one peak to the next valley. It counts open losses as well as closed ones. So a drawdown is not always a loss. You can be in one and still be up on what you paid.
questions.lesson_line: Drawdown is measured from the high, not from where you started.

wrong.A loss below what you paid: A drawdown runs from the peak. You can be in a drawdown and still in profit.
wrong.Money taken out of an account: That's a retirement drawdown, a withdrawal. In trading it means a fall in value.
wrong.The day's high-to-low range: That's one day's range, a volatility number, not a fall in value.

questions.simple: A drop from a peak to a low, measured from the high and not from what you paid.

deeper.example: Investopedia's example: a stock bought at $100 rises to $110, then falls to $80. The drawdown is 27.3%, measured from the $110 peak. The trader's loss is only $20 a share, measured from the $100 they paid.

questions.story: You buy at $40. The stock runs to $60, then falls to $48.
questions.q: Which is true at $48?
choices: A 20% loss on the whole trade
No drawdown, since you're still up
questions.why: A 20% drawdown, but still a profit. Drawdown runs from the peak: $60 down to $48 is 20%. Profit runs from what you paid. You paid $40, and $48 is above it. Investopedia: a drawdown isn't always the same as a loss.
questions.lesson_line: A drawdown can happen inside a winner. It measures what you gave back.

wrong.A 20% loss on the whole trade: You paid $40. At $48 you're still up on the trade.
wrong.No drawdown, since you're still up: Drawdown is measured from the peak, not from your entry.
wrong.A 12% drawdown from the $60 peak: That's the $12 drop read as a percent. Divide it by the $60 peak.

questions.simple: It is a 20% drawdown but still a profit, because drawdown runs from the $60 peak and profit from your $40 buy.

reasons: choices rebalanced (the key was the longest)

questions.q: After a 50% drawdown, a 50% gain gets you back to the peak.
questions.why: False. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back to even. Many people wrongly assume a 50% gain is enough. A percentage loss always needs a bigger percentage gain to repair it. The gain has to be bigger because it starts from a smaller base.
questions.lesson_line: Losses are harder to undo than they look. Keep them small.
questions.simple: False, after a 50% drop you need a 100% gain to get back to the peak.

deeper.trap: Halve an account and it holds half what it did. A 50% gain on that smaller base adds back less than you lost. You are still below the peak. It takes a 100% gain, doubling the half, to get back. That is why big losses are so hard to undo.

questions.q: Your account is down 20% from its peak. What gain takes it back to the high?
questions.why: 25%. After a loss you climb back from a smaller base, so the gain has to be bigger than the loss. A given percent loss always needs a bigger percent gain to break even.
questions.lesson_line: Down 20% needs up 25%. The deeper the hole, the steeper the climb.
questions.simple: You need a 25% gain, because you climb back from a smaller base than the one you fell from.

deeper.example: The climb back is always steeper than the fall. Here, down 20% needs 25%. Every loss needs a bigger gain to repair, so keeping losses small keeps the climb short.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My account fell from its high of $50,000 to $44,000. That fall from the high is a ___.
questions.why: Drawdown. A drawdown is a fall in account value from a peak to the low after it. It is usually quoted as a percent of the peak. It counts open trades as well as closed losses. A gap is a price move, a loss limit is a rule, and a trailing stop is an order.
questions.lesson_line: Track your drawdown from the account's high, not from where you started.
questions.simple: Drawdown, because the account fell from its high of $50,000 to $44,000.

reasons: fixed before (a computed number removed from the sentence)

questions.q: Tap the term that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: I lost my set amount for the day by 11 a.m., so I hit my ___ and stopped trading.
questions.why: Daily loss limit. Fidelity: some traders set a maximum allowable loss for the day and end their activities when they reach it. Schwab calls it a circuit breaker. A monthly limit counts the whole month, not one day. UCT has no daily loss limit. Our limit is monthly: at 8% down in a calendar month, no new trades for the rest of the month.
questions.lesson_line: A daily loss limit ends your trading for the day. UCT's limit is monthly instead.
questions.simple: Daily loss limit, because you lost the amount you set for the day and then stopped trading.

reasons: the why teaches the owner's rulebook B15 and B16 (no daily limit, a monthly 8% limit)

questions.story: Your rule: no new trades once you're down $1,000 in a day. By noon you're down $1,050. At 1 p.m. a great setup appears.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Skip it, but trade after 3 p.m.
Take it to win the loss back
questions.why: Skip it, wait for tomorrow. Your limit is $1,000 and you are down $1,050, so the limit is hit. Fidelity: once you have a limit, have the discipline to observe it. Schwab calls it a circuit breaker. Trading to win it back is the revenge trading Schwab links to many blowups. UCT's own limit is monthly, and it works the same way.
questions.lesson_line: The limit only works as a wall, never as a suggestion.

wrong.Take it to win the loss back: That's revenge trading, which Schwab links to many big blowups.
wrong.Raise today's limit to $2,000: A limit you move when it's hit isn't a limit.
The limit ends your whole day, not just one setup.

questions.simple: Skip it and wait for tomorrow, because a loss limit only works if you obey it once it is hit.

deeper.trap: The trap is the great setup. A limit is only tested when breaking it looks smart. A later trade, a revenge trade and a higher limit all break it. Our monthly rule works the same way. At 8% down in a calendar month, no new trades for the rest of the month.

reasons: the why and deeper teach the owner's rulebook B15 and B16; a daily limit is not a UCT rule

questions.q: What is maximum drawdown?
choices: Your largest loss on one trade
The average of all your drawdowns
questions.why: The biggest peak-to-low drop. Investopedia: the largest decline from a peak to a trough before a new peak. IBKR measures it as a percent fall from the peak value. A bounce that does not make a new high is not a new peak. It measures the whole account, not one trade or one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Max drawdown is the worst stretch your account has lived through.

wrong.Your largest loss on one trade: That's one trade. Max drawdown measures the whole account, peak to low.
wrong.The widest stop you've used: That's a stop setting, not a fall in value.
wrong.The average of all your drawdowns: It's the single worst one, not an average.

questions.simple: The biggest drop from a peak to a low, measured before the account reaches a new high.

deeper.example: Investopedia's example: an account peaks at $750,000, falls, then bounces to $600,000 and falls again. The drop is still measured from $750,000, because $600,000 was not a new high.

questions.story: Your account climbs from $100,000 to $130,000 and falls to $104,000. It bounces to $120,000, drops to $91,000, then makes a new high.
questions.q: What was your maximum drawdown?
questions.why: 30%. Measure from the $130,000 peak to the lowest point, $91,000, before a new high. Investopedia: maximum drawdown is the largest fall from a peak to a trough before a new peak. The $120,000 bounce was not a new high, so it is not the peak.
questions.lesson_line: Max drawdown runs from the highest peak to the lowest low before a new high.

wrong.20%: That's only the first drop. The account fell further before it made a new high.
wrong.24.2%: That starts at the $120,000 bounce. It wasn't a new high, so it isn't the peak.
wrong.9%: That measures from where you started. Drawdown runs from the peak.

questions.simple: Max drawdown is 30%, from the $130,000 high to the $91,000 low before any new high.

deeper.trap: The bounce is the trap. $120,000 looks like a fresh start, but it is below the $130,000 high, so it is not a new peak. Investopedia's own example skips an interim peak of $600,000 for the same reason.

questions.q: What does risk of ruin measure?
choices: Odds of losses too big to recover
Odds that the next trade loses
How far price can gap at the open
questions.answer: Odds of losses too big to recover
questions.why: Odds of losses too big to recover. Investopedia: the probability of losses big enough to make recovery impossible. Tharp sets ruin at the drawdown where you would stop trading, a personal level.
questions.lesson_line: Survival comes first. An edge is worthless once the account can't trade it.

wrong.Odds that the next trade loses: That's one trade. Ruin is about the account surviving a run of them.
wrong.Your largest drawdown so far: That's maximum drawdown, the largest fall already taken. Risk of ruin is about the odds ahead.
wrong.How far price can gap at the open: That's gap risk: a gap past your stop can cost more than you planned on one trade.

questions.simple: Risk of ruin is the chance your losses get so big that the account cannot recover.

reasons: stable definition, two publishers (wording differs, key fits both)

questions.q: Your risk of ruin depends on how much capital you have to cushion your losses.
questions.why: True. Investopedia: risk of ruin depends on how many bets you make and how much capital there is to cushion probable losses. A thin cushion means a normal losing run can finish the account. Tharp says a positive-expectancy method makes money over the long term if the risk level is low enough.
questions.lesson_line: Ruin comes from losses your capital can't absorb. Keep the cushion thick.
questions.simple: True, the more capital you have to absorb a losing run, the lower your odds of ruin.

questions.story: Two traders run the same method, which has a positive expectancy. One risks 1% a trade. The other risks 25%.
questions.q: Which one faces the bigger risk of ruin?
questions.why: The trader risking 25%. Same method and same edge, but very different size. At 25% a trade, a short losing run leaves little capital. Risk of ruin depends on how much capital cushions the losses. Tharp's low-risk idea is sized to survive the worst short-term run. An edge only pays if you are still trading to collect it.
questions.lesson_line: An edge only pays if you're still around to collect it.

wrong.Neither, edge saves both: An edge is an average. Size decides whether you survive the losing runs on the way.
wrong.The trader risking 1%: Small risk keeps the cushion thick, so a losing run hurts far less.
wrong.Both face the same odds: Same method, different size. Ruin depends on how much capital cushions the losses, and 25% a trade leaves little cushion.

questions.simple: The trader risking 25%, because a short losing run at that size leaves little capital to recover with.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a positive expectancy makes you safe. Expectancy is an average over many trades. It pays only if you survive the losing runs on the way. Tharp sizes a low-risk idea for the worst short-term run. UCT's ceiling is 2% a trade, and under 1% is normal.

questions.q: What is portfolio heat?
choices: Total open risk across your trades
How fast your best stock rises
questions.answer: Total open risk across your trades
questions.why: Total open risk across your trades. Tharp: the total open risk in your portfolio at any given time. Seykota and Druz named it the heat of the portfolio. Elder's rule adds up the risk on all open positions the same way. Our rulebook treats total open risk as a guide that varies, not a hard cap.
questions.lesson_line: Portfolio heat is what you lose if every stop hits at once.

wrong.How fast your best stock rises: Heat here means risk, not momentum.
wrong.Your single largest position: That's one position's size. Heat adds up the risk on all of them.
wrong.Your account's monthly drawdown: That's a loss already taken. Heat is risk still open.

questions.simple: Portfolio heat is the total you would lose if every one of your open stops were hit at once.

questions.q: You hold four trades. Each one risks 1.5% of the account to its stop. What is your portfolio heat?
questions.why: 6%. Add up what every open trade loses if its stop is hit: four trades at 1.5% each. Seykota and Druz: 2% on each of five positions is a total heat of 10%. Heat adds up even when each trade looks small.
questions.lesson_line: Know your total heat before you add one more trade.
questions.simple: Your heat is 6%, because four trades that each risk 1.5% add up to 6%.

questions.q: What is concentration risk?
choices: Risk from too much money in one area
Risk from owning too many positions
Risk that your stop order fills too late
Risk of a gap right past your stop
questions.answer: Risk from too much money in one area
questions.why: Risk from too much money in one area. FINRA: the risk of amplified losses from having a large portion of your holdings in one investment, asset class or market segment.
questions.lesson_line: Too much money in one area can amplify your losses.

wrong.Risk from owning too many positions: FINRA's concentration risk comes from too much in one investment or segment, not from too many positions.
wrong.Risk of a gap right past your stop: That's gap risk on one position. Concentration is about how much sits in one area.
wrong.Risk that your stop order fills too late: That's about how a stop order fills. Concentration is about how much sits in one area.

questions.simple: Concentration risk is the bigger loss you can take when too much of your money sits in one area.

questions.story: You hold five chip stocks. Each one risks 1% of the account to its stop.
questions.q: If chips have a bad day, how much of the account is at risk?
choices: About 5%, if all five stops hit
All the money in the stocks
questions.answer: About 5%, if all five stops hit
questions.why: About 5%, if all five stops hit. FINRA: same-industry holdings tend to be highly correlated. What happens to one is likely to happen to the others. Heat adds the risks: five trades at 1% each is 5%.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks in one industry tend to fall together, so their stops can hit together.

wrong.About 1%, one stop will hit: Stocks in one industry tend to move together. When one falls hard, the others likely fall too.
wrong.All the money in the stocks: That's what you invested. Tharp: the amount risked is not the amount invested. Each stop is set to cost 1%.
wrong.About 0.2%, 1% split five ways: Each stock risks its own 1%. Heat adds the risks up; it does not split them.

questions.simple: About 5% is at risk, because chip stocks tend to fall together, so all five stops can hit at once.

deeper.trap: Five tickers feel like five separate bets. FINRA's point is correlation: same-industry stocks tend to move together. A bad day for chips can trigger every stop at once.

questions.q: Owning tech stocks plus a tech fund spreads out your risk.
questions.why: False. FINRA's own example of concentration is tech companies, plus a tech fund, plus tech stocks inside an index fund. Same-industry holdings tend to move together, so the fund adds more of the same bet. Different tickers, same risk.
questions.lesson_line: Look under the hood. Different tickers can carry the same risk.
questions.simple: False, because a tech fund holds more tech, so you own more of the same bet instead of spreading it out.

deeper.trap: The hidden overlap is the trap. FINRA counts the tech stocks inside an index fund you own as part of the same concentration. Look at what each fund holds before you call your book spread out.

questions.q: In Tharp's terms, what is open risk?
choices: Price now to stop, all positions
Entry to stop on your newest trade
Money spent on your open positions
Profit you have not yet sold
questions.answer: Price now to stop, all positions
questions.why: Price now to stop, across all positions. Tharp: the difference between the current price and the stop for all positions you have open. He calls it another word for portfolio heat. Elder's rule, as Incredible Charts explains it, measures each stock from its last month-end close to its stop, times the shares. It is not R, which runs from your entry.
questions.lesson_line: As a winner runs, open risk grows unless your stop follows it.

wrong.Entry to stop on your newest trade: That's the initial risk, R, on one trade.
wrong.Money spent on your open positions: That's what you invested, not what you can lose.
wrong.Profit you have not yet sold: That's open profit, measured from your entry. Open risk runs from the current price down to the stop.

questions.simple: Open risk is what all your positions would lose if they fell from today's price down to their stops.

reasons: stable definition named for Tharp, Elder agrees

questions.q: You own 100 shares bought at $50. They now trade at $62, and your stop is $55. What is your open risk?
questions.why: $700. Open risk runs from today's $62 down to your $55 stop, times 100 shares. Your stop sits above your $50 entry, so a fill at the stop would still be a profit. But the open gain above $55 is still at risk.
questions.lesson_line: Open profit above your stop is still at risk.
questions.simple: Your open risk is $700, because 100 shares could fall from $62 down to your $55 stop.

deeper.example: Here the stop at $55 keeps part of the gain. Every dollar the stock sits above $55 is still exposed. Raising the stop shrinks open risk.

questions.q: What is a breakeven stop?
choices: A stop moved up to your entry price
A stop that trails the session's high
A stop just under the day's low
A target set at a 1R profit level
questions.answer: A stop moved up to your entry price
questions.why: A stop moved up to your entry price. TradeStation places it at the average entry price of the position. Our rulebook moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The aim, in O'Neil's words, is not to let a stock fall back below your purchase price.
questions.lesson_line: A breakeven stop aims to keep a winner from turning into a loser.

wrong.A stop that trails the session's high: A breakeven stop doesn't follow the high. It sits at your entry price.
wrong.A stop just under the day's low: That stop comes from the chart's low. A breakeven stop uses your own entry price.
wrong.A target set at a 1R profit level: That's a profit level, not a stop. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.

questions.simple: A breakeven stop is your stop moved up to the price you paid.

questions.q: With your stop at breakeven, a gap below your entry still fills you at your entry.
questions.why: False. A breakeven stop is a stop market order. When price falls back to entry, a market order is sent. After a gap down, the fill can be well below your entry. The stop price is a trigger, not a guaranteed price. TradeStation also notes its math ignores commission and slippage.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven is a plan to exit at entry, not a promise of no loss.
questions.simple: False: at your entry the stop turns into a market order, and after a gap it can fill well below.

deeper.trap: Breakeven feels like a free trade. It is not. Schwab: after a gap down, the fill can be significantly lower than the stop price. A stop at your entry can still end in a loss.

reasons: Tier 1 fact plus two publishers agree

questions.story: Your breakout is up 1R, so you move the stop to your entry. The stock dips a few cents under your entry and sells you out. Then it rallies hard.
questions.q: What did the breakeven stop cost you here?
choices: It let normal swings stop you out
It locked in a gain on the trade
It capped your upside at your entry
It made the stop a limit order
questions.answer: It let normal swings stop you out
questions.why: It let normal swings stop you out. A stop at your entry sits close to the price. Schwab warns a stop too close can be triggered by regular daily price swings. FINRA notes a quick drop can trigger a stop and the stock can rebound. Our rulebook waits for 2R to 5R, ideally, before moving to breakeven.
questions.lesson_line: An early breakeven stop trades a smaller loss for more shakeouts. We wait for 2R to 5R, ideally.

wrong.It made the stop a limit order: A breakeven stop is still a stop market order. TradeStation: all its stop orders are stop market orders.
wrong.It locked in a gain on the trade: A breakeven stop sits at your entry price. Filled there, it saves you from a loss but keeps no gain.
wrong.It capped your upside at your entry: A stop limits the downside. Your upside was open until the stop sold you out.

questions.simple: Moving the stop to your entry too early lets ordinary dips stop you out before the real move.

deeper.trap: A breakeven stop trades one risk for another. It shrinks the loss if the trade fails, but ordinary dips can now take you out. O'Neil says don't let a worthwhile profit fall back into a loss. Mabe never moves to breakeven. Our rule waits for 2R to 5R, ideally.

questions.q: Which stop rises as the price rises but never moves down?
questions.why: Trailing stop. It follows a rising price up. When the price falls, the stop stays where it is. Schwab: it can move higher but never lower. A breakeven stop sits at your entry, and an initial stop is the first stop, the one that sets R.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop moves one way: with your profit.

wrong.Breakeven stop: That sits at your entry price and stays there.
wrong.Initial stop: That's the first stop, the one that sets R.
wrong.Stop-limit order: That's about the fill price once triggered, not about following the trend.

questions.simple: A trailing stop, because it follows the price up and stays put when the price falls.

questions.q: You set a 20% trailing stop. The stock peaks at $85, then starts to fall. Where is your stop?
questions.why: $68. The stop trails 20% under the $85 high, and it stays there as the stock falls. A trailing stop measures from the highest price, not from your entry. Tharp's example: a 25% trail under a $60 high sits at $45 and is never moved back down.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop measures from the high, not from your entry.
questions.simple: Your stop is at $68, because it sits 20% under the $85 high and never moves down.

deeper.counter: A percent trail is one way to trail. Our own default is not a percent. We sell on a close below the 10-day average for fast movers, or the 21-day for steadier ones.

questions.story: You bought at $30. The stock ran to $60, and your 25% trailing stop now sits at $45. Then the stock turns down.
questions.q: What does the stop lock in if it fills at $45?
questions.why: $15 a share, half the gain. You paid $30 and the stop sells at $45, so you keep $15 a share. At the $60 high the gain was $30, so the stop keeps half. That's Tharp's own example. The trail is 25% of the price, not 25% of the gain.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop gives some gain back so you can stay for the rest.

wrong.$30 a share, the whole gain: The stop sits 25% under the high, so part of the gain goes back.
wrong.$45 a share, the stop price: $45 is the price you sell at, not your profit. You paid $30, so you keep $15 a share.
wrong.$22.50 a share, 75% of the gain: That takes 25% off the $30 gain. The trail is 25% off the $60 price, which puts the stop at $45.

questions.simple: The stop locks in $15 a share, half the gain, because you sell at $45 after paying $30.

deeper.trap: The trail only moves one way. Tharp: never move it backward. If the stock falls from $60 to $50, the exit stays at $45. Lowering it to give the trade room would hand back the profit the trail was built to keep.

questions.q: A wider trailing stop gives back more profit when the trend finally turns.
questions.why: True. Set too far away, a real reversal eats more of your profit before the stop is hit. Set too close, normal swings stop you out before the trend is done. Schwab warns about both sides. This compares two trails both still open at the turn.
questions.lesson_line: Too wide gives back profit. Too tight gets shaken out. Weigh both when you set the trail.
questions.simple: True, a trail set far away lets the price fall further before you are out, so you give back more.

deeper.counter: A wider trail is not always worse. A tight trail can stop you out on a normal dip and miss the rest of the run. The wide trail loses more only at the final turn. Our default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits our rule.
questions.sentence: Hold your winners by selling partials into strength and ___ the rising moving averages.
questions.why: Trailing. In the owner's words: hold your winners by selling partials into strength and trailing the rising moving averages.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength. Trail the rest under the rising averages.

questions.q: What does ATR measure?
choices: How much a stock typically moves
How far price is from average
questions.answer: How much a stock typically moves
questions.why: How much a stock typically moves. Wilder's average true range is an average of the true range, usually over 14 days. On a daily chart, an ATR of $1.18 means an average range of $1.18 a day. It measures volatility, the size of the moves.
questions.lesson_line: ATR tells you how far a stock normally moves in a day.

wrong.Average volume over 14 days: That's a volume average. ATR uses price ranges.
wrong.Your average loss per trade: That comes from your trade log, not the chart.
wrong.How far price is from average: That's a stretch measure. ATR averages the size of each day's range.

questions.simple: How much a stock typically moves, because ATR averages the size of each day's true range.

questions.q: A rising ATR tells you the stock is heading higher.
questions.why: False. ATR measures volatility, not direction. Big ranges come with strong moves either way. A stock falling hard can show a rising ATR, just as a stock rising hard can. ATR says how big the moves are, never which way.
questions.lesson_line: ATR says how big the moves are, never which way.
questions.simple: False, ATR only shows how big the moves are, and it rises in a sharp fall too.

questions.story: Stock A trades at $300 with a daily ATR of $6. Stock B trades at $20 with a daily ATR of $1.50.
questions.q: Which one moves more for its price?
questions.why: B, about 7.5% a day. ATR is in dollars, so a high-priced stock shows a bigger number. StockCharts: ATR is not shown as a percent of the close, so raw ATRs can't be compared across price levels. B's $1.50 is 7.5% of $20. A's $6 is a much smaller share of $300.
questions.lesson_line: Compare ATR as a percent of price. Dollars alone mislead.

wrong.A, ATR is bigger: A $6 ATR on a $300 stock is a small move for its price.
wrong.About the same: For its price, B moves several times as much as A.
wrong.B, 1.5% a day: That reads the $1.50 ATR as a percent. ATR is in dollars, and $1.50 on a $20 stock is 7.5%.

questions.simple: Stock B moves more for its price, because its $1.50 range is 7.5% of $20, far more than A's share of $300.

deeper.trap: A bigger ATR number is not a bigger move. StockCharts warns that ATR values are not comparable across price levels. Divide ATR by the price before you compare how jumpy two stocks are.

questions.q: Our Launchpad stop goes under the 21-day and 50-day averages. How far under the lower one?
choices: A quarter of an ATR below
Right on it, with no cushion
questions.answer: A quarter of an ATR below
questions.why: A quarter of an ATR below. Our Launchpad plan puts the stop under both the 21-day and 50-day averages, a quarter of an ATR below the lower one. It is the setup's own stop, set from the averages and ATR, not a flat percent.
questions.lesson_line: Our Launchpad stop: under both averages, plus a quarter ATR.

wrong.Three full ATRs below it: That's the long Chandelier Exit: three ATRs under the 22-day high, a trailing stop.
wrong.A flat 10% of the price: Our Launchpad stop comes from the averages and ATR, not a flat percent.
wrong.Right on it, with no cushion: The plan adds a quarter-ATR cushion under the lower average.

questions.simple: Our Launchpad stop sits a quarter of an ATR under the lower of the 21-day and 50-day averages.

reasons: house setup plan not yet reviewed against the rulebook

questions.story: Yesterday the stock closed at $50. Today it gaps up: high $54, low $52.50.
questions.q: What is today's true range?
questions.why: $4.00. True range is the largest of three distances: high to low, high to the prior close, or low to the prior close. Here they are $1.50, $4.00 and $2.50. After a gap up, high to the prior close wins.
questions.lesson_line: True range is the largest of three distances. Check all three.

wrong.$1.50: That's only today's high minus low. It misses the gap from yesterday's close.
wrong.$2.50: That's low to the prior close. The high is farther from it.
wrong.$5.50: That adds two of the distances together. True range is the largest one, not a sum.

questions.simple: True range is $4.00, because after the gap up the high is farthest from yesterday's $50 close.

questions.q: What is the name of a trailing stop set a multiple of ATR under the highest high?
questions.why: Chandelier Exit. Chuck LeBeau's exit places a trailing stop a multiple of ATR under the highest high since entry. StockCharts' version hangs three ATRs under the 22-period high. As the high rises, the stop rises with it. A jumpier stock has a bigger ATR, so its stop sits further away.
questions.lesson_line: The Chandelier Exit lets volatility set the trail.

wrong.Breakeven stop: That sits at your entry price.
wrong.Initial stop: That's your first stop, set at entry.
wrong.Moving-average trail: That trails a moving average. The Chandelier Exit uses the high minus ATRs.

questions.simple: The Chandelier Exit, because it hangs a trailing stop a few ATRs under the highest high.

questions.q: The 22-day high is $80 and the 22-day ATR is $2.50. Where is a long Chandelier Exit set 3 ATRs down?
questions.why: $72.50. StockCharts' long Chandelier Exit is the 22-day high minus three times the 22-day ATR: $80 less three times $2.50. It is a trailing stop based on ATR, so it hangs under the high and its distance grows with volatility.
questions.lesson_line: Chandelier Exit: the 22-day high minus three ATRs, by default.
questions.simple: The exit sits at $72.50, three ATRs of $2.50 under the $80 high.

questions.story: You trail jumpy tech stocks with a 3-ATR Chandelier Exit. Normal pullbacks keep stopping you out before the trend resumes.
questions.q: What should you change on your next trade?
questions.why: A higher ATR multiplier. StockCharts: volatile stocks may need a higher multiplier to reduce whipsaws, and it names techs. Set it before you enter. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. A wider stop costs more per share if hit, so buy fewer shares from the new stop distance.
questions.lesson_line: Give a jumpy stock more room, and buy fewer shares to pay for it.

wrong.A flat 2% stop instead: A flat percent ignores how much this stock swings.
wrong.A smaller ATR multiplier: That tightens the stop. You'd get shaken out even more.
wrong.Same stop, half the shares: Fewer shares cut the dollars lost, but the same trail still shakes you out.

questions.simple: Use a higher ATR multiplier on the next trade, because a jumpy stock needs more room, then buy fewer shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is widening the stop on a trade you already hold. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Set the wider trail at entry, and buy fewer shares so the dollars at risk stay the same.

questions.q: What does volatility-based position sizing do?
choices: Same share count on every trade
Size set by your win rate
questions.why: Smaller size for jumpier stocks. Tharp's percent volatility model caps the volatility in each position, usually measured by ATR, at a set percent of equity. Investopedia: higher volatility may require smaller positions. So a stock that swings more gets fewer shares, not more.
questions.lesson_line: Let the stock's swing set the size, so each position moves the account about the same.

wrong.Bigger size for jumpier stocks: Backwards. Bigger swings call for fewer shares.
wrong.Same share count on every trade: That ignores both the stop and the swing.
wrong.Size set by your win rate: Win rate doesn't measure how much a stock moves.

questions.simple: It buys a smaller size in jumpier stocks, so each position swings the account by about the same amount.

questions.q: A trailing stop can be set a fixed percent or a dollar amount away from the price.
questions.why: True. The SEC says a trailing stop price is a defined percentage or dollar amount above or below the market price. As the price moves your way, the stop follows by that amount. When the price moves against you, it stays fixed.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop sits a set percent or dollar amount from the price.
questions.simple: True, a trailing stop can sit a set percent or a set dollar amount away from the price.

reasons: one source only (SEC Investor.gov bulletin), which refused WebFetch (403) on 2026-11-12, so it was not re-read this run

questions.q: After a 10% loss, you need an 11% gain to get back to even.
questions.why: True. Every loss needs a bigger gain to repair it. Down 10% needs 11%, and down 50% needs 100%.
questions.lesson_line: Losses are repaired by bigger gains. Down 10% needs 11%.

questions.q: A high win rate alone does not prove a method makes money.
questions.why: True. Win rate counts how often you win, not how much. Investopedia: a trader who wins more often can still have a losing strategy when the losses are much bigger than the gains. Tharp notes that some systems with a high hit rate lose money through occasional large losses.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate alone proves nothing. The size of the losses matters too.
questions.simple: True, if the losing trades are much bigger than the winners, a high win rate can still lose money.

questions.q: TradeStation's breakeven stop only takes effect once the trade reaches a set profit.
questions.why: True. TradeStation's breakeven stop places a stop at your average entry price once the profit passes a set floor. Until then it does nothing, so in a given trade it may never take effect. UCT moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.
questions.lesson_line: A breakeven stop waits for a set profit before it moves to entry.
questions.simple: True, this breakeven stop only goes in once the trade shows the profit you set, so it may never kick in.

deeper.counter: Not every trader uses a breakeven stop. Dave Mabe never moves a stop to breakeven. O'Neil says not to let a worthwhile profit fall back below your purchase price. Our rule: move it to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R, ideally.

reasons: the key rests on one source (TradeStation)
the why and deeper teach the owner's rulebook B19 (breakeven at 2R to 5R)

questions.q: True range counts the gap from the prior close, which the day's high-to-low range misses.
questions.why: True. A range from the high to the low alone misses volatility from gaps. Wilder built true range to capture it. True range is the largest of three distances: high to low, high to prior close, and low to prior close. So a gap open shows up in true range.
questions.lesson_line: True range includes the gap from the prior close, so gaps count.
questions.simple: True, true range adds the distance from the prior close, so a gap counts in the stock's range.

questions.q: What risk per trade does our rulebook call normal?
choices: Under 1% of the account a trade
2% of the account on every trade
1.5% of the account on every trade
Up to 5% a trade on top setups
questions.answer: Under 1% of the account a trade
questions.why: Under 1% of the account a trade. Our rulebook: under 1% is normal, and 1.5% is the most any grade uses. 2% is the absolute ceiling, not the normal.

wrong.2% of the account on every trade: 2% is our absolute ceiling, not our normal. Under 1% is normal.
wrong.Up to 5% a trade on top setups: Our ceiling is 2% a trade. Even the best grade uses 1.5% at most.
wrong.1.5% of the account on every trade: 1.5% is the most any grade uses, a top, not the normal. Under 1% is normal.

questions.simple: Our normal risk is under 1% of the account a trade, and 2% is the most we ever risk.
questions.lesson_line: Our normal risk is under 1% a trade. 2% is the ceiling.

conflicts: Risk/reward naming. Investopedia (riskrewardratio.asp) writes the ratio risk first, as potential loss / potential gain, so 'a 1:2 risk/reward ratio' means risk $1 to make $2 and lower is better. Van Tharp's glossary entry 'Reward-to-Risk Ratio' means yearly return / maximum drawdown, or average win / average loss. Schwab's 5 Elements page says 'risk-to-reward ratio ... how many dollars do you expect to gain for each dollar you commit to the position', which mixes it up with return on capital. The file keys only what the ratio compares (entry to stop vs entry to target, q19) and the dollars made per dollar risked (q20), and names 1:3 as Investopedia's way of writing it.

Win/loss ratio. Investopedia defines it as winning trades / losing trades; Schwab's 5 Elements page calls 'the percentage of your trades that have been profitable' a win/loss ratio. Investopedia's own example also says a 12/18 = 0.67 ratio 'means that you are losing 67% of the time' while giving the win rate as 40% (the loss rate is 60%). Not keyed: the file teaches 'win rate' (Tharp and Investopedia agree: winning trades out of all closed trades) and never asks win/loss ratio.

Open risk vs heat base. Tharp's glossary measures open risk from the CURRENT price to the stop and calls it 'another word for portfolio heat'; Seykota and Druz describe heat as the bet size risked per instrument; F9.06 notes R is measured from the entry. The file measures open risk from the current price (q48, q49), keys heat only as the total of what every stop would lose (q43, q44, q46), and never keys which base heat uses.

Heat caps. Tharp's glossary says portfolio heat 'generally should not exceed 20%'; Elder's rule (Incredible Charts) caps open risk at 6%; docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 5 says 10% but marks it 'App cap', not an owner answer. No cap is keyed anywhere in this file.

Investopedia, Trailing Stops (Henry Hoenig): its NVDA example writes '$99 (110 - (11 x 0.10))' (the arithmetic is 110 - 110 x 0.10), and it says swing trading 'by definition is not about riding a trend'. Neither is cited; only its definitional lines on stops set too close or too far, and on moving-average trails, are used.

Investopedia, How Stop-Loss Orders Help Limit Investment Losses and Risk: its earnings example says the stop 'triggers at $90, limiting the loss' after a gap down, contradicting its own gap paragraph, the SEC and FINRA. Only the gap paragraph (f102) is cited.

Investopedia, Understanding the 2% Rule (James Chen): its AAPL example writes '$50,000 x 0.02%' (2% is meant) and '4% loss ($1,000 / $30)' (67 shares x $30 is about $2,010, which is about 4% of $50,000), and its 'Practical Example' treats 2% as an allocation cap, contradicting its own definition (risk per trade). Only the definition (f99), the gap/slippage line (f100) and the volatility-sizing line (f101) are cited; q26 builds its own gap example with a calc.

True range. Van Tharp's ATR glossary lists the third true-range term as 'today's low minus yesterday's close' without the absolute value; Investopedia and StockCharts use absolute values. True range (q62) is keyed on Investopedia and StockCharts only; Tharp's ATR entry is not cited.

ATR smoothing. Investopedia's key takeaway says ATR is 'typically derived from the 14-day simple moving average' of true range; StockCharts uses Wilder's smoothing ([prior ATR x 13 + current TR] / 14). The file says only that ATR averages the true range, usually over 14 days.

Breakeven stops. TradeStation defines the breakeven stop (a stop at the average entry price once a set profit is reached); O'Neil (AAII) says not to let a worthwhile profit fall back below the purchase price; Dave Mabe (IBKR Campus) never moves a stop to breakeven. The file keys the definition (q50) and both costs, gaps (q51) and shakeouts (q52), and never says when to move to breakeven or that you always should.

Risk of ruin. Investopedia defines it as the probability of losses too big to recover from; Tharp's glossary defines 'ruin' as the drawdown at which you would stop trading (a personal level, not necessarily zero). q40's key ('odds of losing too much to recover') fits both, and the why gives both.

Seykota and Druz (s23): the line 'If you risk too much, you eventually run to ruin' is the magazine's introduction to the article on its product page, not necessarily the authors' words; the file credits it to the magazine's page in the claim and never quotes it as Seykota's.

R-multiple by name. Only Van Tharp defines 'R-multiple' among the sources found: the Van Tharp Institute pages and his own January 2007 article in Stocks & Commodities (an independent publisher, Technical Analysis, Inc.). No Investopedia, Schwab, Fidelity, StockCharts or IBKR page defining the term was found. The definitional R and R-multiple questions also cite Investopedia's matching 'trade risk is the dollar difference between the entry price and the stop-loss'. Checker to judge whether Tharp in two publications meets the two-publisher rule; the computed R-multiple items (q07, q09) carry calcs.
Chandelier Exit creator: Investopedia spells him 'Chuck LeBeau', StockCharts 'Charles Le Beau'; the same person. The file uses 'Chuck LeBeau'.

Not used: the owner's drawdown ladder in docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 4 (quoted, but flagged there for the owner to confirm as house numbers; F9.04 covers it), the 0.25% to 2% risk range and 'flat-risk sizing' in section 1 (not marked as the owner's answer), and 'pilot', 'ceiling', 'flat risk' and 'structure stop' from the UNITS-foundations row (house words with no owner-ruled definition in the repo; the units_plan entry, which overrides the row, does not list them).
